identification.title: Central Asia flood hazard discharge data
identification.description: Central Asia flood hazard discharge data. Developed as part of the Strengthening Financial Resilience and Accelerating Risk Reduction in Central Asia program. (https://www.gfdrr.org/en/program/SFRARR-Central-Asia)

point_of_contact.name: Risk Engineering and Development (RED), Pavia, Italy

data_quality.data_notes: These data have been derived on a regional scale for the purpose of consistent regional multi-country hazard and risk assessment. Application of this information on smaller scales should be done with care. Importantly on a local scale, it is often the case that more detailed history and hazard information is required to perform such hazard and risk modelling, particularly were applied to dimension mitigation structures or strategies.

geographical_extent.description: The data include gauge stations from the five Central Asian Countries (which includes Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan).

related_links_and_publications: Task 3 Flood Hazard Assessment Report - Regionally consistent risk assessment for earthquakes and floods and selective landslide scenario analysis for strengthening financial resilience and accelerating risk reduction in Central Asia (SFRARR Central Asia disaster risk assessment)

Resources.name: Annual maxima discharge data
Resources.description: Dataset of annual maxima discharge (m3/s) from different gauges in Central Asia between 1909 and 2020.

Resources.name: Discharge hazard curves uncertainty bounds
Resources.description: Discharge hazard curves uncertainty lower bounds calculated for all 78,000 virtual stations (simulation points) for 2,5,10,20,50,100,200,500 and 1,000 years return time. The uncertainty analysis was carried out by comparing the modelled discharge extreme values distributions after bias correction with the observed ones (both obtained through a GEV fitting). Absolute values of percent errors were computed on pairs of observed vs. simulated flows at fixed return periods (5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 years) for every river section where observed data were available. Then, for every return period, the empirical 90% percentile of all percent errors in all gauged stations was computed. The corresponding values of percent errors were used to obtain lower and upper bounds of  discharge extreme values distributions at gauged sections. For ungauged sections, a similar procedure was put in place, but rather than comparing extreme values distributions from simulations and observations (obviously not available at ungauged sections), the comparison was done on distributions before and after the bias correction. The final result was, again, lower and upper bounds of  discharge extreme values distributions. ID stands for the virtual station ID. noData: “-9999”. UNits: m3/s

Resources.name: Discharge hazard curves
Resources.description: Discharge hazard curves calculated for all 78,000 virtual stations (simulation points) for 2,5,10,20,50,100,200,500 and 1,000 years return time via extreme value analysis which included generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution fitting, temporal anc spatial shifts detection, extreme values adjustment and extrapolation. Both observed and simulated annual maximum discharge values were used to fit the GEV via the non-linear least squares method. ID stands for the virtual station ID. noData: “-9999”. UNits: m3/s

Resources.name: Daily discharge data
Resources.description: Dataset of daily discharge (m3/s) from different gauges in Central Asia between 1936 and 2020.

Resources.name: Discharge hazard curves climate change (2080 scenario)
Resources.description: Discharge hazard curves for the 2080 scenario (climate change) calculated for all 78,000 virtual stations (simulation points) for 2,5,10,20,50,100,200,500 and 1,000 years return time. The climate change scenario simulation was carried out by adopteding change factors to the ERA5-Land precipitation and temperature based on the pdf comparison of the current climate and 1971-2100 projection (we used MPI-ESM-MR GCM). We used a pdf matching technique to change the distributions of the current ERA5-Land variables. Eventually, the entire modeling chain composed of hydrological modeling (TOPKAPI), extreme values analysis was performed to produce the fluvial flood hazard curves under 2080 conditions. ID stands for the virtual station ID. noData: “-9999”. UNits: m3/s

collections.collection_title: Gender Spatial Data - Small Island States
collections.collection_description:
Project Page: https://worldbank.github.io/GEEST/README.html

As part of the “Geospatial Assessment of Women Employment and Business Opportunities in the Energy Sector” project, open-source Gender-related spatial data was collected for 31 Small Island Developing States (SIDS) across the globe, resulting in curated and thoroughly documented geodatabases (GDBs) that are now ready to be explored! Fifty-nine spatial layers were identified and then researched for each country, covering the following categories: Demographics and Population | Renewable Energy | Energy Access | Education | Jobs and Finance | Digital Inclusion | Transportation | Safety | Amenities | Climate/Earth | Law/Policy/Government.

Data and dataset subscriptions managed by the Library Network on agriculture, business, economics, energy, finance, health, risk, water, and more..

The LinkedIn-World Bank partnership offers data to help governments and researchers understand rapidly evolving labor markets with detailed and dynamic data. It allows leaders to benchmark and compare labor markets across the world; analyze skills, occupations, migration, and industries; and leverage real-time data to make policy changes.Visualizations for many of these data are available at linkedindata.worldbank.org
Collection of merchandise trade data available to World Bank staff.
This collection includes datasets associated with research organized under the Bank, Policy Research Working Papers.
This collection contains data on disaster and climate risk assessments curated by the Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery (GFDRR).
This collection presents software tools and models developed by the World Bank to support monitoring, planning, programming and the economic evaluation of roads and highways works.

This spatial database, a product of the South Asia Region Chief Economist's (SARCE) Office, presents data collected from official sources and harmonized into different spatial levels. Data includes economic and environmental data across 12 topic areas, and includes data from four countries in South Asia (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, and Nepal) for both 2001 and 2011.

A collection of country Small Area Estimation (SAE) and Poverty Mapping that contains papers, shapefiles, and datasets produced through partnerships between the World Bank and country statistics offices.

This collection consists of datasets compiled and created by the World Bank Data Lab in response to a request by the Syria Economic Monitor Team to explore alternative data sources to better understand changing trends in trade and economic activity, focusing on: surface cross-border transport routes, changes in observed agricultural production, observed nighttime lights, and reported conflict.

From Data to a Water-Secure World for All. World Bank Water Data surrounding the three pillars of Sustain Water Resources, Deliver Services and Build Resilience.

The World Development Report 2021: Data for Better Lives explores the tremendous potential of the changing data landscape to improve the lives of poor people, while also acknowledging its potential to open back doors that can harm individuals, businesses, and societies. To address this tension between the helpful and harmful potential of data, this Report calls for a new social contract that enables the use and reuse of data to create economic and social value, ensures equitable access to that value, and fosters trust that data will not be misused in harmful ways. The data used in the WDR2021 are curated as a collection here.

The World Development Report 2022: Finance for an Equitable Recovery examines the central role of finance in the economic recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. In doing so, it looks into the consequences of the crisis most likely to affect emerging economies and proposes a set of policies to mitigate the interconnected financial risks stemming from the pandemic and to steer economies toward a sustainable and equitable recovery. The data used in the WDR2022 are curated as a collection here.
The World Settlement Footprint Collection includes country datasets describing the evolution of the built-area across the globe at a ~30m resolution.
